extracted.intended_audience: contracting officers, government contract attorneys, contractors and sureties working on U.S. federal government contracts
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and practical rules for entering into, approving, and enforcing supplemental contracts and handling extras, extensions, waivers, and substitutions under United States government contracts (particularly construction and supply contracts). Covers when modifications are permissible, what constitutes adequate consideration in the interest of the United States, and limits on officials' authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts may alter payment terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplementary contract may be made to provide for payment in full for individual units (e.g., each building) even though the original contract aggregated prices and withheld retainage until final completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is desirable to make payment in full for each building when completed, a supplementary contract can be made providing for such payment (example: Fort Hancock buildings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changed site conditions justify supplemental contract/annulment
rubrics_metrics.description: If conditions encountered (e.g., deep peat bog) make the work as specified impracticable, the original contract may be annulled or modified by supplemental contract to authorize alternative methods or materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where test borings misled drafters and original construction method cannot be executed, a supplemental contract annulling or modifying the original contract is legally permissible (case: Illinois & Mississippi Canal—peat bog).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts to provide governmental aid at contractor's expense
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental contract may authorize government departments to aid or supplement a contractor's operations, with the contractor charged actual cost and such cost deducted from his payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When contractor performance is unsatisfactory, a supplemental agreement allowing the Engineer Department to assist and charging the contractor the actual cost is permissible (example: Savannah River improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts to reimburse for government-caused inability to perform
rubrics_metrics.description: If the government fails to provide necessary design/specifications or otherwise prevents contractor performance, a supplemental contract may annul the original contract and reimburse the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contractor unable to make campaign badges because Government failed to provide suitable designs—supplemental contract to reimburse allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental modifications to add required features
rubrics_metrics.description: Original contracts can be modified by supplemental contract to add features (e.g., sliding supports for files/drawers) when parties desire the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supplemental contract may simply modify the original to add items reasonably connected with the work (case cited Oct. 4, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for extra time due to government delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor may be granted compensation by supplemental contract for additional time and attention required because of delay in execution caused by government failure or error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental contracts have been used to compensate for government-caused delays (cases: Nov. 3, 1910; Nov. 21, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite supplemental contracts with surety to complete work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where contractor cannot complete work but surety is willing to finish, a tripartite supplemental contract among the United States, the original contractor, and the surety may be made whereby the surety completes the work using contractor's plant and receives payments, and the contractor releases claims against the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible provided total payments do not exceed original contract amount and contractor releases the U.S. from claims (cases cited Oct. 8, 1901; July 25, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government contractual warranty for conditions of law (duties) and supplemental relief
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contract contains a provision (warranty) that goods 'will be admitted free of customs duties' and subsequent change in law imposes duties, the United States is liable for duties and may enter a supplemental contract to pay an additional price to cover duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A repeal of law imposing free admission does not violate contract but creates liability to pay duties paid by contractor; supplemental contract to cover duties permissible (cases Aug. 18 & Dec. 29, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract for extension and bond reduction due to government delay
rubrics_metrics.description: If contractor delayed by government fault and additional work requires reduced bond, supplemental contract may extend time, provide for a reduced bond, and reimburse additional expenses including premium on new bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible where additional work will be sufficiently secured by smaller bond; include reimbursement for expenses and bond premium (C. 28472, June 6, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchase of contractor's plant using appropriations without advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain appropriation statutes (e.g., River and Harbor Act), funds may be applied to purchase supplies or contractor plant without advertising when most economical, enabling supplemental contract for termination and purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice under the Act permits purchase without advertising for river and harbor works; a supplemental contract may be entered for termination and purchase of contractor's plant (C. 2215, May 12, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute security/bond may allow release of retained percentages when tests impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contractual practical test becomes impossible (e.g., winter passed), retained percentages may be paid if contractor provides a bond guaranteeing the plant will meet the specified test at the next feasible time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: steam-heating plant installed after winter; retained percentages paid on bond that plant will conform next winter (C. 13001, July 22, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra work practicable only by contractor may be ordered without advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Where extra work, in addition to contracted work, is required by the officer in charge and is practicable of performance only by the contractor, such extra work may be performed without advertising and the contractor paid its reasonable value in absence of an agreed price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision references: C. 6901 (Mar. 4, 1899) and C. 10920 (Aug. 3, 1901).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected subsurface conditions and extras entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: If excavations reveal unexpected conditions (quicksand, deeper footings required) and officer authorizes change in foundation character, the extra cost constitutes an 'extra' recoverable by contractor (or quantum meruit when beyond reasonable limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor may be paid for new kind of foundation as extra (C. 987Jf., Feb. 25, 1901; C. 19437, Apr. 2, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government failure to supply promised materials entitles contractor to extra compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Government agrees to furnish materials (e.g., crushed stone) but fails to supply sufficient quantities, the contractor may recover reasonable compensation for increased expense of obtaining materials elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contractor hauling stone from more distant point—extra compensation allowed (C. 23546, Nov. 3, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual mistake in contract wording permits compensation for extra work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where mutual error in contract wording caused contractor to perform work not intended to be covered, and facts establish contractor's claim, he is entitled to compensation for the extra work performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor not estopped by his conduct if facts support claim (C. 22238, Oct. 24, 1907).

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of written-approval requirement by officer in charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract requires modifications to be approved before performance, but extra work is performed without such approval with the consent of the officer in charge, the written-approval provision may be waived and a supplemental contract should be approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance with officer's consent can constitute waiver (C. 23501, June 27, 1908; C. 10449, May 18, 1901; C. 19487, Apr. 2, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to order extras — orders by subordinate vs. authorized officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional work ordered by a subordinate without authority is voluntary service and generally not recoverable; but alterations or additions ordered by an officer authorized to contract create an implied contract to the extent of the benefit the Government received, even if written order was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Barlow v. U. S., 35 Ct. Cls. 514: orders by authorized officer bind both Government and contractor; oral orders by principal-agent may waive written-order requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract must be 'in the interest of the United States'
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental contract cannot be made if it is against the interest of the United States; sufficient consideration or benefit to the Government must exist to justify the modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative considerations include: acceptance at reduced price of usable nonconforming material; relinquishment of bona fide claims; settlement with insolvent contractor to secure funds and early completion; temporary reduction of contractual requirements to expedite work; advance payment for material upon delivery to speed construction; substitution of equivalent materials or price reductions when substitute inferior (multiple cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of items requires equivalence or price adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting a different article (e.g., different brand of caster or baled hay for loose hay) by supplemental contract is permissible provided the substitute is 'as good as' the contracted-for article, or a reduction in price is provided so the contract is not against the United States' interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Legmount' for 'Faultless' caster allowed if equally good; otherwise reduce price (C. 23511, June 29, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to a specific date — requirements and preservation of Government remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract may be extended to a specific date by supplemental contract without advertisement if not against the United States' interest; if no new consideration is provided, the supplemental contract should expressly preserve contractor liability for liquidated damages or other actual damages resulting from delay, to protect the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extension does not give new consideration, supplemental contract should preserve liabilities (examples and recommendations cited). Extensions may also be indefinitely waived by officer in charge with required approvals, leaving other contract provisions in force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts after expiration of time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after the expiration of the contractual time limit, if the contract remains in force a supplemental contract extending the time to a specified date may be entered into without advertising where the interests of the United States will not be prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: C. 14649 (July 1, 1903); C. 15818 (Jan. 22, 1904). Similar approach for delayed delivery start dates (C. 7484; C. 24207).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of waiver of time limit — other provisions remain in force
rubrics_metrics.description: A waiver of the time limit (as opposed to extension to a specific date) leaves all other provisions of the contract in force; partial payments, liquidated damages, and other contractual provisions continue to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waiver implies an implied contract to complete within a reasonable time; partial payments may be made per contract terms after waiver (C. 15818, Jan. 22, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for inspection/superintendence expenses when original contractor causes delay
rubrics_metrics.description: If an original contractor's failure causes total completion time (including successor contractor) to exceed the original contract period, the original contractor is liable for inspection and superintendence expenses attributable to the time exceeding the original period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where initial contractor given additional time did not create 'extension' within contract meaning, deduction for such expenses may be improper; but if total time exceeds contracted period, extra expenses are Government loss attributable to original contractor (C. 2400, July 8, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of surety's liability during extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond that binds surety 'as well during any period of extension of said contract...as during the original term' may or may not cover mere extensions of commencement without completion-date extension; whether surety bound depends on interpretation of 'extension of contract' in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not always clear that mere postponement of commencement equals an extension of the contract for bond purposes (C. 13906; C. 20423).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on departmental heads' authority to release rights without consideration or statute
rubrics_metrics.description: A department head executing public contracts acts as agent of the United States and, absent express statutory authority, cannot legally relinquish rights or property of the Government by supplemental contract (e.g., increase compensation, release from performance) if such action would be against the Government's interest, unless adequate consideration passes to make it in the Government's interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War and similar officials lack power to release contractor from obligations, discharge debts, pay extra compensation for a bad bargain, or otherwise grant relief without proper consideration or congressional authority (numerous cases and Attorney General opinions cited).
